records.title: Cultural Consequences of Connectivity
records.heading: Connected does not mean identical
records.text:
Connected does not mean identical
Diffusion creates connections while preserving local agency and difference.
People borrowed useful practices without abandoning all earlier identities. Chinese institutions influenced Korea, Japan, and Vietnam, but local governments and social groups adapted them. Muslim communities in East Africa developed forms of language, architecture, and family life shaped by African and oceanic contexts.
Power shaped cultural exchange. Rulers could sponsor a religion or technology, merchants could carry practices to a port, and local communities could accept, modify, or resist them. The same tradition could gain different meanings in different places.
A strong comparison therefore identifies both a shared connection and a meaningful difference. Similar architecture, a shared religion, or a common technology is evidence of contact; it is not by itself proof of direct political control.

records.title: Environmental Consequences of Connectivity
records.text:
Environmental Consequences of Connectivity
How connected exchange changed crops, populations, disease patterns, labor, and land use across Afro-Eurasia.
Exchange could support food production and population growth while also spreading disease and increasing pressure on land; outcomes depended on local conditions and choices.
The same routes that moved luxury goods and beliefs also moved plants, animals, microbes, and farming knowledge. Environmental consequences are part of connectivity, not a separate story outside economic history.
records.excerpt: How connected exchange changed crops, populations, disease patterns, labor, and land use across Afro-Eurasia.

records.title: Environmental Consequences of Connectivity
records.heading: Crops crossed regions
records.text:
Crops crossed regions
Crop diffusion changed possibilities, but farmers and environments determined the outcome.
Champa rice, a quick-ripening and relatively resilient variety associated with mainland Southeast Asia, spread into parts of China. Bananas moved from Southeast Asia to Africa through maritime connections. Citrus and other crops circulated across Afro-Eurasian markets.
A crop’s movement depended on farmers, climate, soil, water, and local knowledge. People adapted growing methods, selected varieties, and changed land use. A crop could be important without being the only cause of population change.
Crops also carried cultural and economic meanings. New foods could enrich diets, support settlement, or become market products. Explain the route and local conditions rather than assuming a new crop had the same impact everywhere.

records.title: Environmental Consequences of Connectivity
records.heading: Food, population, and land use
records.text:
Food, population, and land use
Environmental change is produced by interactions among crops, people, institutions, and physical conditions.
Higher yields could support population growth and urbanization when farmers had suitable land, water, labor, and political stability. In parts of China, rice expansion supported settlement and specialized work. Similar relationships occurred in other regions, but timing and scale varied.
Population growth could increase cultivation, irrigation, deforestation, and grazing. These changes sometimes supported cities and sometimes strained soils, forests, and water supplies. Human responses included migration, technological adjustment, and political regulation.
Do not turn agriculture into a one-step equation. Food availability, disease, conflict, taxation, and labor arrangements all influenced whether a population grew and whether land use remained sustainable.

records.title: Environmental Consequences of Connectivity
records.heading: Pathogens moved with mobility
records.text:
Pathogens moved with mobility
Connectivity can spread disease, but the path, scale, and consequences must be qualified.
Trade, military movement, migration, and animal contact created pathways for infectious disease. The bubonic plague spread through connected regions in the fourteenth century, causing severe losses in multiple parts of Eurasia. Exact routes and regional effects require careful evidence.
Caravanserai and ships brought people and animals into close contact, which could increase opportunities for transmission. This does not mean one institution alone caused an epidemic. Disease dynamics depended on hosts, vectors, climate, timing, and local public health conditions.
Avoid presenting one precise origin story or claiming that a region was completely untouched when evidence is mixed. The defensible historical point is that intensified mobility helped pathogens cross distances and societies experienced the consequences unevenly.

records.title: Environmental Consequences of Connectivity
records.heading: Demographic shocks changed labor
records.text:
Demographic shocks changed labor
Disease changed economic relationships through demographic shock, but labor outcomes depended on institutions and power.
Large epidemics reduced populations in affected areas and disrupted farms, cities, families, and states. Where labor became scarce, surviving workers could sometimes bargain for better pay or conditions. These effects varied by region, status, law, and political response.
A population decline could reduce production and tax revenue while raising the relative value of labor. Employers, landlords, and governments attempted different responses, including wage controls, coercion, migration, and changes in land use.
The effects were not simply economic. Disease altered religious practice, family structures, political legitimacy, and people’s understanding of their environment. Historical explanations should connect demographic change to institutions rather than predict one universal result.

records.title: Environmental Consequences of Connectivity
records.heading: Societies also changed environments
records.text:
Societies also changed environments
Environmental consequences are reciprocal: networks reshape environments, and environmental changes reshape networks.
Expanded agriculture and trade could intensify deforestation, overgrazing, soil erosion, and water use. Such pressures contributed to the decline or relocation of some settlements, but single-cause explanations are usually too simple. Environmental stress interacted with politics, disease, and production.
Connectivity could therefore create feedback. A growing market encouraged more cultivation; intensified cultivation changed the land; environmental decline then affected yields, migration, and trade. The same network could spread a useful crop and a harmful pathogen.
A later comparison with the Columbian Exchange can help students see a larger pattern, but it belongs to later history. Keep Unit 2 examples within c. 1200–1450 and label later developments as context only.

records.title: Comparison of Economic Exchange
records.text:
Comparison of Economic Exchange
A method for comparing the Silk Roads, Indian Ocean, and trans-Saharan networks with specific evidence and explained reasoning.
All three networks connected producers and consumers and depended on political and environmental conditions, but their routes, technologies, goods, and state structures produced meaningful differences.
The networks developed from older routes and settlements. The period from 1200 to 1450 intensified exchange across Afro-Eurasia, making comparison useful while still requiring attention to overlap and regional variation.
records.excerpt: A method for comparing the Silk Roads, Indian Ocean, and trans-Saharan networks with specific evidence and explained reasoning.

records.title: Comparison of Economic Exchange
records.heading: How to compare historically
records.text:
How to compare historically
Comparison requires a common dimension, specific evidence, and a reasoned explanation of the relationship.
A comparison begins with a shared category: route geography, transport, commercial practice, state involvement, or cultural consequence. It then identifies a similarity or difference and explains why it existed. Listing one fact about each network is not yet an argument.
For example, all three networks depended on political stability to some degree, but the form of protection differed. A comparison becomes stronger when it names the institution, identifies the mechanism, and explains the result.
Good comparisons also define their limits. Networks overlapped, varied over time, and contained many communities. Treating them as sealed boxes hides the very connections the unit asks students to explain.

records.title: Comparison of Economic Exchange
records.heading: Shared causes and effects
records.text:
Shared causes and effects
Shared processes are useful only when supported with specific mechanisms and examples.
Demand for goods, agricultural production, commercial knowledge, and state protection helped all three networks grow. Merchants, diplomats, missionaries, and migrants moved along them, and trading cities became important nodes.
All networks spread cultural practices and created opportunities for rulers and merchants. They also carried risk: war, environmental stress, and disease could disrupt exchange. Similar effects do not mean identical experiences or equal benefits.
A defensible shared-cause claim must use more than a vague phrase such as “trade increased.” Explain how a technology, institution, or political decision changed the conditions of exchange in at least two networks.

records.title: Comparison of Economic Exchange
records.heading: Geography changes the route
records.text:
Geography changes the route
Transport and geography shaped what moved, when it moved, and which places became important.
The Silk Roads crossed deserts and mountain passes, encouraging caravan travel and exchange in valuable, portable goods. Indian Ocean routes used ships and monsoon timing to connect coastal and island markets. Trans-Saharan routes depended heavily on camel caravans and oases.
These differences affected what was practical. Ships could carry larger or heavier loads than many overland caravans, while desert caravans needed water planning and load-bearing saddles. Neither network was technologically simple; each required specialized knowledge.
A route’s geography also influenced which cities grew. An oasis, river crossing, strait, or deepwater port could become a service node, but political decisions and security determined whether that advantage lasted.

records.title: Comparison of Economic Exchange
records.heading: States and communities
records.text:
States and communities
Exchange depended on both states and ordinary specialists, whose roles differed by network.
States supported exchange through protection, taxation, ports, roads, customs, and diplomacy. Mali benefited from West African gold and trade revenue; Malacca gained from its strategic strait; Mongol khanates shaped large portions of overland Eurasia.
Communities also sustained exchange. Diasporic merchants, caravan specialists, sailors, farmers, artisans, and local brokers made networks work. A ruler could claim authority over a route, but everyday expertise remained distributed among many groups.
Cultural outcomes followed these political and social arrangements. Islam, Buddhism, language, architecture, and scientific knowledge circulated through different institutions. Comparison should ask who carried an idea and how local people changed it.

records.title: Comparison of Economic Exchange
records.heading: From comparison to argument
records.text:
From comparison to argument
A comparison becomes an argument when evidence is connected to a claim and qualified where the pattern varies.
A thesis should make a defensible claim about degree, cause, or significance. For example: all three networks expanded through political support and specialized transport, but the Indian Ocean’s seasonal maritime system created different port communities than the overland routes.
Evidence must do work. Naming Malacca and Timbuktu shows knowledge; explaining how a strait and a desert city generated different revenue and services supports the comparison. Reasoning connects the example to the claim.
Complex arguments recognize a qualification. A network can be mostly maritime and still rely on inland routes; a state can protect trade and also exploit merchants or conquered people. Nuance is historical accuracy, not indecision.

records.title: Empires Expand
records.text:
Empires Expand
How gunpowder weapons, military organization, and rivalries shaped the growth of the Ottoman, Safavid, Mughal, Qing, and Songhai states.
Land-based empires grew when rulers combined new gunpowder weapons with disciplined armies, effective revenue systems, and alliances with local elites.
Gunpowder had spread from China across Eurasia before 1450. In the following centuries, rulers who could afford cannons, muskets, and trained soldiers built some of the largest states the world had yet seen.

records.title: Empires Expand
records.heading: Gunpowder and military organization
records.text:
Gunpowder and military organization
Gunpowder weapons mattered most when states could pay for them and organize soldiers to use them.
Cannons could break city walls that had resisted older siege methods. When the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II took Constantinople in 1453, giant cannons pounded its defenses for weeks. Muskets gave infantry a way to defeat cavalry when soldiers fired in disciplined ranks.
Firearms were expensive. A ruler needed revenue to buy cannons, pay gunners, and keep soldiers trained all year. The Janissaries, the Ottoman standing infantry, show how a state paired new weapons with a permanent professional force.
Historians sometimes call the Ottoman, Safavid, and Mughal states gunpowder empires. The label highlights a real change, but it can hide the importance of cavalry, diplomacy, and tax collection.
Rulers with steady revenue bought cannons and paid standing armies, which let them take fortified cities and defeat rivals, which brought more land and taxes to pay for still larger armies.
Do not write that guns alone built these empires. A strong answer links weapons to the money, organization, and alliances that made them useful.

records.title: Empires Expand
records.heading: Ottoman, Safavid, and Mughal expansion
records.text:
Ottoman, Safavid, and Mughal expansion
Three Muslim dynasties built large empires in Southwest and South Asia, each by combining conquest with ways of governing diverse subjects.
The Ottoman Empire grew from a small state in Anatolia. After 1453, Constantinople, renamed Istanbul over time, became its capital. Selim I conquered the Mamluk sultanate of Egypt and Syria in 1517, and Suleiman I, who ruled from 1520 to 1566, pushed into Hungary and besieged Vienna in 1529.
The Safavid Empire began in 1501 when Ismail I took power in Persia. Shah Abbas I, who ruled from 1588 to 1629, reorganized the army with firearms and enslaved soldiers from the Caucasus and made Isfahan a splendid capital.
The Mughal Empire began in 1526 when Babur defeated the Sultan of Delhi at Panipat using field guns. His grandson Akbar, who ruled from 1556 to 1605, expanded across northern India and drew Hindu Rajput princes into his service.
The Ottomans did not convert most of their Christian subjects, and the Mughals did not convert most of their Hindu subjects. Muslim rule and a Muslim majority are different things.

records.title: Empires Expand
records.heading: The Qing dynasty
records.text:
The Qing dynasty
The Qing were a land-based empire that conquered China and then expanded it, ruling as a small Manchu minority.
The Manchus, from northeast of the Great Wall, organized their society into military banners. In 1644, after rebels took Beijing and the last Ming emperor died, Manchu armies entered China and founded the Qing dynasty.
Qing emperors expanded far beyond Ming borders. They took Taiwan in 1683 and, in the 1750s, defeated the Zunghar Mongols and added Xinjiang. The Qianlong emperor, who ruled from 1735 to 1796, presided over the empire at its largest.
Ming weakness and rebellion opened Beijing to the Manchus, and the banner armies then allowed the Qing to defeat rivals on the steppe and push China's borders into Central Asia.

records.title: Empires Expand
records.heading: Rivalries between states
records.text:
Rivalries between states
Political, economic, and religious motives drove conflict between empires, often at strategic frontiers.
Empires competed for land, trade routes, and prestige. The Safavids and Mughals fought for Kandahar, a fortress on the main route between Persia and India. The Ottomans and Safavids fought for decades, and their rivalry was sharpened by the Sunni and Shi'a divide.
In West Africa, the Songhai Empire controlled Gao and Timbuktu and taxed the trans-Saharan trade. In 1591 an army sent by the Moroccan sultan Ahmad al-Mansur crossed the Sahara and used firearms to defeat Songhai at the Battle of Tondibi. Morocco gained less gold than it hoped, and the region broke into smaller states.
Not every rivalry was religious. Kandahar was fought over by two Muslim dynasties for strategic and commercial reasons.

records.title: Empires: Administration
records.text:
Empires: Administration
How rulers used officials, soldiers, religion, monuments, and taxes to legitimize and consolidate power.
Rulers kept large empires together by recruiting loyal officials and soldiers, linking their authority to religion and spectacle, and finding reliable ways to collect taxes.
Conquest created empires, but administration kept them. Rulers from Europe to East Asia faced the same problems: finding loyal servants, persuading subjects to obey, and paying for armies and courts.
records.excerpt: How rulers used officials, soldiers, religion, monuments, and taxes to legitimize and consolidate power.

records.title: Empires: Administration
records.heading: Loyal officials and soldiers
records.text:
Loyal officials and soldiers
Rulers sought officials and soldiers whose loyalty depended on the ruler, not on their own family wealth.
The Ottomans used the devshirme, a system in which Christian boys from the Balkans were taken from their families, converted to Islam, and trained to serve the sultan. The most talented became administrators; many others joined the Janissaries. Because they had no noble family to support them, they depended on the sultan.
In Japan, the Tokugawa shogunate, established in 1603, moved samurai into castle towns and paid them fixed rice stipends. The alternate attendance system required daimyo, the regional lords, to live part of the time in Edo and leave their families there as hostages.
The Qing kept the Ming examination system, so Chinese scholars staffed most offices. Many top posts were shared by one Manchu and one Han Chinese official.
Rulers feared powerful nobles, so they recruited servants who owed everything to the throne, which reduced the chance that officials would build rival power bases.
The devshirme was coercive. Describing it only as a path to opportunity leaves out that boys were taken from their families by force.

records.title: Empires: Administration
records.heading: Religion and the right to rule
records.text:
Religion and the right to rule
Rulers tied their authority to religious ideas so that obedience seemed a sacred duty.
Many European monarchs claimed divine right, the belief that God chose kings and that resisting them was resisting God. Louis XIV of France, who ruled from 1643 to 1715, became a model of absolutism, ruling without calling France's representative assembly.
In Songhai, Askia Muhammad, who ruled from 1493 to 1528, promoted Islam, appointed Muslim judges, and made a pilgrimage to Mecca. Earlier, Mexica rulers had linked their power to sacred duties, including human sacrifice to the sun god.
Ottoman sultans took the title of caliph and protected the holy cities of Mecca and Medina after 1517. Safavid shahs presented themselves as leaders of Shi'a Islam.
Religious legitimacy did not mean everyone shared the ruler's faith. Askia Muhammad's promotion of Islam left rural religious practice largely unchanged.

records.title: Empires: Administration
records.heading: Art and monumental architecture
records.text:
Art and monumental architecture
Monuments and art turned royal power into something people could see.
The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal as a tomb for his wife, blending Persian, Indian, and Islamic designs. The architect Sinan designed the Süleymaniye Mosque for Suleiman I. Louis XIV moved his court to Versailles in 1682 and turned daily life there into ceremony centered on the king.
Qing emperors commissioned portraits showing themselves as Confucian scholars, Buddhist patrons, and Manchu warriors. In the Americas, the Inca had covered the Temple of the Sun at Cusco with gold.
Rulers needed subjects and rivals to see their power, so they spent heavily on monuments, which displayed wealth and piety and gave the dynasty a lasting public image.

records.title: Empires: Administration
records.heading: Collecting revenue
records.text:
Collecting revenue
Revenue systems relied on intermediaries, which made collection possible but also created room for abuse.
In Mughal India, zamindars, local landholders, collected taxes from peasants and kept a share. Ottoman rulers increasingly used tax farming, selling the right to collect certain taxes to bidders who paid in advance.
The Mexica had recorded tribute owed by conquered towns in painted lists. In Ming China, reforms in the late 1500s merged many taxes and labor duties into one payment in silver, which increased Chinese demand for silver from Japan and the Americas.
Tax farming raised money quickly but let collectors squeeze peasants. Do not describe any system as simply efficient without naming its costs.

records.title: Empires: Belief Systems
records.text:
Empires: Belief Systems
How the Protestant and Catholic reformations, the Sunni and Shi'a rivalry, and the rise of Sikhism changed belief systems from 1450 to 1750.
Belief systems split and changed in this period, and rulers often turned religious differences into political boundaries.
Christianity, Islam, and the religions of South Asia were centuries old by 1450. New printing technology, the ambitions of rulers, and the work of reformers produced lasting divisions and one new religion.
records.excerpt: How the Protestant and Catholic reformations, the Sunni and Shi'a rivalry, and the rise of Sikhism changed belief systems from 1450 to 1750.

records.title: Empires: Belief Systems
records.heading: The Protestant Reformation
records.text:
The Protestant Reformation
Religious criticism became a lasting division when printing spread it and rulers adopted it for their own ends.
In 1517 Martin Luther, a German monk, challenged the sale of indulgences, grants said to reduce punishment for sins. He argued that salvation came through faith and that the Bible, not Church tradition, was the highest authority. The printing press spread his writings quickly.
German princes who supported Luther gained control over churches and Church lands in their territories. The Peace of Augsburg in 1555 allowed each prince in the Holy Roman Empire to choose Lutheranism or Catholicism for his lands. Other reformers, such as John Calvin, built separate Protestant churches, and in 1534 Henry VIII made himself head of the Church of England.
Anger at Church practices and the spread of printed criticism led many to reject papal authority, and rulers who saw political and financial gain backed the reformers, which made the split permanent.
The Reformation was not only about belief. Princes and kings supported it partly to gain power and property, so explain both motives.

records.title: Empires: Belief Systems
records.heading: The Catholic Reformation
records.text:
The Catholic Reformation
Catholic reform strengthened the Church in many regions but did not restore Christian unity in western Europe.
The Catholic Church responded with reform and renewal. The Council of Trent, from 1545 to 1563, reaffirmed Catholic teachings and ordered bishops to stop abuses. The Society of Jesus, or Jesuits, founded in 1540, opened schools and sent missionaries around the world.
Religious divisions fed wars. The Thirty Years' War, from 1618 to 1648, began as a conflict between Protestant and Catholic states in the Holy Roman Empire and became a struggle among Europe's great powers. The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 confirmed that rulers would decide the religion of their own states.
The Catholic Reformation was not only a reaction. It also renewed Catholic education and missions that reached Asia and the Americas.

records.title: Empires: Belief Systems
records.heading: Sunni and Shi'a rivalry
records.text:
Sunni and Shi'a rivalry
The Sunni and Shi'a split was centuries old, but Ottoman and Safavid rivalry made it a border between states.
Ismail I, founder of the Safavid dynasty in 1501, made Twelver Shi'ism the state religion of Persia and pressed Sunni subjects to convert. The Ottomans, who were Sunni, saw Safavid influence among Anatolian tribes as a danger.
At the Battle of Chaldiran in 1514, Ottoman cannons and muskets defeated Safavid cavalry. Warfare continued until a treaty in 1639 fixed a lasting border. Political rivalry hardened the religious line between a mostly Shi'a Persia and mostly Sunni Ottoman lands.
Safavid rulers used Shi'ism to unify their state and win followers, the Ottomans treated this as a threat, and decades of war turned the religious divide into a political frontier.

records.heading: The rise of Sikhism
records.text:
The rise of Sikhism
Sikhism developed from the meeting of religious traditions in South Asia into a new faith.
Sikhism began in the Punjab with Guru Nanak, who lived from 1469 to 1539. He taught devotion to one God and rejected caste distinctions in worship. Community kitchens served meals to everyone, whatever their caste.
Scholars note links between Sikh teachings and both Hindu bhakti devotion and Islamic Sufism. Over time Sikhs developed their own scripture, the Adi Granth, compiled in 1604, and their own institutions.
Sikhism drew on older traditions but is a distinct religion, not a branch of Hinduism or Islam.

records.title: Comparison in Land-Based Empires
records.text:
Comparison in Land-Based Empires
How the Ottoman, Safavid, Mughal, and Qing empires compared in expansion, legitimacy, and their treatment of diverse subjects.
Land-based empires shared common problems, but they solved them in different ways depending on their rulers, subjects, and resources.
Comparison is a core AP skill. A strong comparison names the same feature in two empires, gives evidence for both, and explains why the similarity or difference mattered.
records.excerpt: How the Ottoman, Safavid, Mughal, and Qing empires compared in expansion, legitimacy, and their treatment of diverse subjects.

records.title: Comparison in Land-Based Empires
records.heading: Comparing expansion
records.text:
Comparing expansion
Similar weapons led to different military systems shaped by each empire's society.
All four major land empires used gunpowder weapons, but in different ways. The Ottomans built a large salaried infantry, the Janissaries. The Mughals used field cannons at Panipat but relied heavily on cavalry and alliances with Rajput princes. The Qing banners combined cavalry traditions with firearms.
Each empire expanded at frontiers where rivals were weak or divided. The Qing defeated the Zunghar Mongols, the Ottomans advanced into Hungary, and the Mughals pushed south into the Deccan.
A comparison needs both sides. Saying the Ottomans used Janissaries is a description; adding how the Mughals differed makes it a comparison.

records.title: Comparison in Land-Based Empires
records.heading: Comparing legitimacy
records.text:
Comparing legitimacy
Empires that spoke to several audiences at once were better able to hold diverse subjects.
Rulers combined religion, ceremony, and monuments. Ottoman sultans claimed the title of caliph, Safavid shahs led Shi'a Islam, Mughal emperors built grand tombs and mosques, and Qing emperors presented themselves as Confucian rulers to Chinese subjects and as Buddhist patrons to Tibetans and Mongols.
Each dynasty was a ruling minority. Inclusion of local elites, such as Rajputs in Mughal service or Han Chinese officials in the Qing bureaucracy, made rule more stable.
Because rulers governed populations very different from themselves, they adopted multiple ways of claiming authority, which helped them win the cooperation of different groups.

records.title: Comparison in Land-Based Empires
records.heading: Comparing religious policy
records.text:
Comparing religious policy
Religious policy ranged from accommodation to pressure, with real effects on stability.
The Ottomans allowed Christian and Jewish communities to keep their own religious leaders and courts for family matters, while non-Muslims paid the jizya tax. Akbar abolished the jizya in 1564 and brought Hindu nobles into high office. Aurangzeb restored it in 1679, and revolts followed.
The Safavids, by contrast, pressed for conversion to Shi'ism. Religious policy could unify a ruling group, but it could also alienate subjects.
Tolerance in this period did not mean equality. Ottoman non-Muslims paid extra taxes and faced legal limits even while practicing their faith.

records.title: Technological Innovations from 1450 to 1750
records.text:
Technological Innovations from 1450 to 1750
How tools, ship designs, and knowledge of winds and currents, much of it borrowed, made transoceanic voyages possible.
Europeans combined navigational knowledge and tools from Asia and the Islamic world with new ship designs, which made voyages across open oceans possible.
Before 1450, sailors in the Indian Ocean, South China Sea, and Mediterranean had long used compasses, lateen sails, and seasonal winds. Atlantic Europeans built on this knowledge.

records.title: Technological Innovations from 1450 to 1750
records.heading: Borrowed knowledge
records.text:
Borrowed knowledge
European exploration rested on knowledge gathered across Afro-Eurasia.
The magnetic compass came from China. The astrolabe, refined by scholars in the Islamic world, measured the height of stars to find latitude. The lateen sail, a triangular sail used in the Indian Ocean and Mediterranean, let ships sail closer to the wind.
European mapmakers also drew on Greek, Arabic, and Chinese geographic knowledge. Printing spread new maps and sailing guides quickly.
Do not describe these tools as European inventions. The AP framework stresses that knowledge from the Classical, Islamic, and Asian worlds made European voyages possible.

records.title: Technological Innovations from 1450 to 1750
records.heading: New ships
records.text:
New ships
Ship design responded to the goals of exploration, warfare, and cheap cargo transport.
Portuguese builders developed the caravel, a small ship with square and lateen sails that could explore coasts and sail against the wind. Larger carracks carried more cargo and guns for long trading voyages.
The Dutch later built the fluyt, a cargo ship designed to carry large loads with a small crew. Lower shipping costs helped the Dutch dominate European trade in the 1600s.
Better ships lowered the cost and risk of long voyages, which made regular ocean trade profitable and encouraged states and merchants to invest in it.

records.title: Technological Innovations from 1450 to 1750
records.heading: Winds and currents
records.text:
Winds and currents
Understanding wind patterns turned dangerous voyages into repeatable routes.
Sailors learned that Atlantic winds move in large circles. Portuguese captains returning from West Africa swung far west to catch winds blowing toward Europe. Columbus used the trade winds that blow west near the Canary Islands.
In the Indian Ocean, monsoon winds had long set the rhythm of trade. When Vasco da Gama reached East Africa in 1498, he hired a local pilot who knew the route to India.
Europeans did not discover the monsoons. They learned the Indian Ocean system from sailors who had used it for centuries.

records.title: Exploration: Causes and Events from 1450 to 1750
records.text:
Exploration: Causes and Events from 1450 to 1750
Why European states sponsored ocean voyages, and how Portuguese, Spanish, English, French, and Dutch exploration unfolded.
European states sponsored exploration to gain wealth, spread Christianity, and gain advantage over rivals, especially by reaching Asian trade without Muslim or Venetian middlemen.
Asian spices, silk, and porcelain reached Europe through Ottoman, Egyptian, and Venetian merchants who took large profits. Atlantic kingdoms looked for routes of their own.
records.excerpt: Why European states sponsored ocean voyages, and how Portuguese, Spanish, English, French, and Dutch exploration unfolded.

records.title: Exploration: Causes and Events from 1450 to 1750
records.heading: Why states sponsored voyages
records.text:
Why states sponsored voyages
Exploration was a state project driven by economic, religious, and political goals.
Rulers wanted gold, spices, and new sources of revenue. They also hoped to spread Christianity and outflank Muslim rivals. Voyages were expensive and risky, so they usually needed royal backing.
Mercantilism, the idea that a state grows strong by exporting more than it imports and accumulating gold and silver, encouraged rulers to claim colonies and control trade.
High prices for Asian goods and the profits taken by middlemen made a direct sea route valuable, so rulers funded voyages, which led to new routes and colonies.
Do not reduce exploration to curiosity. States paid for voyages because they expected wealth and power.

records.heading: Portugal reaches Asia
records.text:
Portugal reaches Asia
Portugal pioneered a sea route around Africa to Asia's markets.
Prince Henry of Portugal sponsored voyages down the West African coast in the early 1400s. Bartolomeu Dias rounded the southern tip of Africa in 1488, and Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in India in 1498.
The sea route let Portugal trade for spices without Venetian or Ottoman middlemen. Portugal soon built fortified trading posts along the coasts of Africa and Asia.

records.heading: Spain crosses the Atlantic
records.text:
Spain crosses the Atlantic
Spanish voyages connected the Americas to Europe and, through the Pacific, to Asia.
Christopher Columbus sailed for Spain in 1492, hoping to reach Asia by sailing west, and reached the Caribbean. The Treaty of Tordesillas in 1494 divided newly claimed lands between Spain and Portugal.
The expedition begun by Ferdinand Magellan sailed around the world from 1519 to 1522. Spain went on to conquer the Mexica and Inca empires and built a vast American empire funded by silver.
Columbus did not prove the world was round; educated Europeans already knew that. His error was underestimating the distance to Asia.

records.heading: English, French, and Dutch voyages
records.text:
English, French, and Dutch voyages
Northern voyages failed to find a route to Asia but opened fisheries and the fur trade.
John Cabot, sailing for England, reached Newfoundland in 1497. Jacques Cartier explored the St. Lawrence River for France in the 1530s. They searched for a northwest passage to Asia and did not find one.
Instead, northern Atlantic voyages led to rich fisheries and a fur trade with Indigenous peoples. French and Dutch traders exchanged metal goods and cloth for beaver pelts.

records.title: Columbian Exchange
records.text:
Columbian Exchange
How the transfer of diseases, crops, and animals between hemispheres after 1492 transformed populations, diets, and environments.
The Columbian Exchange reunited the biology of two hemispheres, causing a catastrophic population collapse in the Americas and new food supplies in Afro-Eurasia.
For thousands of years, the Americas and Afro-Eurasia had developed separate plants, animals, and diseases. After 1492, ships carried all three across the Atlantic.
records.excerpt: How the transfer of diseases, crops, and animals between hemispheres after 1492 transformed populations, diets, and environments.

records.title: Columbian Exchange
records.heading: Disease and demographic collapse
records.text:
Disease and demographic collapse
Epidemic disease was the deadliest part of the exchange and shaped the labor systems that followed.
Smallpox, measles, and influenza had no history in the Americas, so Indigenous people had no acquired immunity. A smallpox epidemic struck Tenochtitlan in 1520. Historians estimate that the Indigenous population of the Americas fell by as much as 90 percent within a century.
Disease combined with war, forced labor, and displacement. The collapse helped Spanish conquest and created labor shortages that colonists filled with enslaved Africans.
New diseases killed huge numbers of Indigenous people, which weakened resistance to conquest and led colonists to import enslaved Africans to replace lost labor.
Disease was unintentional, but conquest, forced labor, and violence also caused deaths. A strong answer names both.

records.heading: Crops and animals
records.text:
Crops and animals
New foods fed growing populations in Afro-Eurasia, and new animals transformed American environments.
Maize, potatoes, and manioc, first grown in the Americas, became staple foods across Europe, Africa, and Asia. Some historians link them to population growth in the 1700s.
Europeans brought wheat, sugarcane, horses, cattle, and pigs to the Americas. Horses changed hunting and warfare on the Great Plains, while grazing animals reshaped landscapes.

records.title: Columbian Exchange
records.heading: Plantations and the environment
records.text:
Plantations and the environment
Plantation agriculture linked the Columbian Exchange to slavery and environmental change.
Sugarcane, originally from Asia, became the main plantation crop of Brazil and the Caribbean. Plantations cleared forests, exhausted soils, and relied on the forced labor of enslaved Africans.
Enslaved Africans also brought knowledge and crops, including rice cultivation in parts of the Americas. The exchange moved people and knowledge, not only plants and animals.
The exchange was not equal. Indigenous Americans suffered population collapse, while Europeans gained land, crops, and wealth.

records.title: Maritime Empires Established
records.text:
Maritime Empires Established
How European states built trading-post empires, joint-stock companies, and colonies, and how some African and Asian states grew through new trade.
European maritime empires grew through fortified trading posts, chartered companies, and conquest, while some African and Asian states used new trade to grow stronger.
Once sea routes were known, European states and merchants competed to control them. Their methods ranged from naval force at Asian ports to conquest of entire American empires.
records.excerpt: How European states built trading-post empires, joint-stock companies, and colonies, and how some African and Asian states grew through new trade.

records.title: Maritime Empires Established
records.heading: Trading-post empires
records.text:
Trading-post empires
Trading-post empires used naval force to profit from trade without governing large territories.
Portugal seized fortified ports such as Goa in 1510 and Malacca in 1511. It required Asian ships to buy passes and pay duties, enforcing the system with armed ships.
Most Indian Ocean trade remained in Asian hands, and land empires such as the Mughals were barely affected. A trading-post empire controlled points on the coast, not whole regions.
Do not describe Portugal as ruling India. It held a handful of coastal forts while powerful Asian states ruled the interior.

records.heading: Joint-stock companies
records.text:
Joint-stock companies
Joint-stock companies combined private investment with state-like powers.
The English East India Company, chartered in 1600, and the Dutch East India Company, or VOC, chartered in 1602, raised money by selling shares to investors. These joint-stock companies spread the risk of long voyages among many owners.
Governments gave the companies the right to build forts, keep armies, and make treaties. The VOC, based at Batavia on Java from 1619, used force to control the spice trade.
Long voyages were costly and risky, so merchants pooled money in joint-stock companies, which let them fund fleets and armies and compete for control of Asian trade.

records.heading: Conquest in the Americas
records.text:
Conquest in the Americas
In the Americas, Europeans built territorial empires rather than trading posts.
Hernán Cortés, with tens of thousands of Indigenous allies, defeated the Mexica between 1519 and 1521. Francisco Pizarro captured the Inca ruler Atahualpa in 1532 during a civil war within the empire.
Spain built a land empire in the Americas with viceroys, colonial courts, and the Catholic Church. Portugal colonized Brazil, while France, England, and the Netherlands founded colonies in North America and the Caribbean.
A small number of Spanish soldiers did not conquer the Mexica alone. Indigenous allies, disease, and internal divisions were essential.

African states and Atlantic trade
Some African states grew stronger by taking part in Atlantic trade, including the slave trade.
The Kingdom of Kongo established ties with Portugal in the 1480s. King Afonso I adopted Christianity but protested Portuguese slave raiding. The Asante kingdom, rising around 1700, sold gold and enslaved war captives to Europeans for firearms and cloth.

records.title: Maritime Empires Maintained and Developed
records.text:
Maritime Empires Maintained and Developed
How coerced labor, the Atlantic slave trade, the silver trade, and Asian trade restrictions shaped maritime empires.
Maritime empires depended on coerced labor and global flows of silver, while powerful Asian states set limits on European activity.
Colonies produced silver, sugar, and other goods for world markets. Producing them required huge numbers of workers, most of whom were forced to work.
records.excerpt: How coerced labor, the Atlantic slave trade, the silver trade, and Asian trade restrictions shaped maritime empires.

records.title: Maritime Empires Maintained and Developed
records.heading: Coerced labor in Spanish America
records.text:
Coerced labor in Spanish America
Spanish colonial wealth depended on coerced Indigenous labor.
The encomienda system gave Spanish colonists the right to demand labor and tribute from Indigenous communities. After abuses and population collapse, the crown restricted it, and haciendas came to rely on workers bound by debt.
Spain adapted the Inca mit'a into a forced labor draft for the silver mines of Potosí, discovered in 1545. Many workers died in dangerous mines.
The Spanish mit'a used an Inca name, but it served colonial mining and was far deadlier than the Inca labor system.
records.excerpt: Spanish colonial wealth depended on coerced Indigenous labor.

records.heading: The Atlantic slave trade
records.text:
The Atlantic slave trade
The Atlantic slave trade forcibly moved millions and built a racial hierarchy into colonial societies.
Plantations in Brazil and the Caribbean imported enslaved Africans in huge numbers. About 12.5 million Africans were forced across the Atlantic, and nearly 2 million died during the Middle Passage.
Chattel slavery made enslaved status hereditary and tied it to race. Enslaved Africans nonetheless preserved languages, beliefs, and skills that shaped American cultures.
Indigenous population collapse and the profits of sugar led planters to buy enslaved Africans, which expanded the slave trade and created racially defined slavery in the Americas.

Silver and global trade
American silver created the first truly global trade network, centered on Chinese demand.
After Spain founded Manila in 1571, the Manila galleons carried American silver across the Pacific to trade for Chinese silk and porcelain. Japan also exported large amounts of silver to China.
China's demand for silver, partly because taxes were paid in silver, pulled the Americas, Asia, and Europe into one trade network. Silver also caused inflation in Spain.

records.heading: Asian states set limits
records.text:
Asian states set limits
Strong Asian states controlled the terms of European trade.
In the 1630s, Tokugawa Japan banned Christianity, expelled the Portuguese, and limited European trade to the Dutch at Nagasaki. By the 1750s, the Qing limited European merchants to the port of Canton.
These policies did not end trade. They let powerful Asian states control it and limit foreign religious and political influence.
Japan was not completely isolated. It traded with the Dutch, China, and Korea under strict control.

records.title: Internal and External Challenges to State Power from 1450 to 1750
records.text:
Internal and External Challenges to State Power from 1450 to 1750
How Indigenous peoples, colonized societies, nobles, and rival groups resisted expanding states.
As states expanded and centralized their power, many groups resisted, from Indigenous peoples facing colonial rule to nobles defending their privileges.
Expanding empires demanded labor, taxes, and religious conformity. Those demands produced revolts inside empires and resistance at their edges.
records.excerpt: How Indigenous peoples, colonized societies, nobles, and rival groups resisted expanding states.

records.title: Internal and External Challenges to State Power from 1450 to 1750
records.heading: Resistance to colonial rule
records.text:
Resistance to colonial rule
Colonized peoples resisted through revolt, diplomacy, and escape.
In the Pueblo Revolt of 1680, communities in present-day New Mexico, led by Popé, rose against Spanish rule and drove colonists out for more than a decade. Spanish demands for labor and attacks on Pueblo religion had fueled the revolt.
In west-central Africa, Queen Nzinga of Ndongo and Matamba resisted Portuguese expansion for decades. Enslaved people who escaped plantations formed maroon communities in Jamaica, Brazil, and elsewhere.
Colonial demands for labor and suppression of local religion led to resentment, which turned into armed revolt when communities could unite.
records.excerpt: Colonized peoples resisted through revolt, diplomacy, and escape.

records.title: Internal and External Challenges to State Power from 1450 to 1750
records.heading: Challenges from within
records.text:
Challenges from within
Centralizing rulers faced resistance from elites and rival groups as well as from peasants.
In France, nobles and Paris officials rose against royal power in the Fronde from 1648 to 1653. In India, the Maratha leader Shivaji built an independent kingdom and fought the Mughals in the 1670s. In Russia, Cossack revolts challenged the tsar's authority.
These challenges sometimes weakened states, as the Marathas weakened the Mughals. Other times, as in France, the ruler emerged stronger.
Not all resistance came from the bottom. Elites such as French nobles resisted when centralization threatened their power.

records.text:
Changing Social Hierarchies from 1450 to 1750
How new hierarchies based on ancestry formed in colonial societies, and how empires treated religious and ethnic groups.
Empires both kept older hierarchies and created new ones, most strikingly in the Americas, where ancestry and race shaped a person's legal and social position.
Conquest and the slave trade mixed European, African, and Indigenous peoples in the Americas. Rulers in Asia governed diverse populations with hierarchies of their own.

records.title: Changing Social Hierarchies from 1450 to 1750
records.heading: The casta system
records.text:
The casta system
Colonial hierarchies tied status to ancestry and race.
Spanish American society ranked people largely by ancestry. Peninsulares, born in Spain, held the highest offices. Creoles, of Spanish descent but born in the Americas, were wealthy but often excluded from top posts. Mestizos and mulattoes had mixed ancestry. Indigenous people and enslaved Africans were near the bottom.
Categories were not always fixed in practice. Wealth, occupation, and reputation could change how people were classified.
Conquest and the slave trade produced populations of mixed ancestry, which led colonial elites to create ranked categories that protected their own privileges.
Do not treat the casta system as identical to the caste system of South Asia. The casta system was based on ancestry in a colonial society.

records.title: Continuity and Change from 1450 to 1750
records.text:
Continuity and Change from 1450 to 1750
What changed and what stayed the same as sea routes connected the world from 1450 to 1750.
Ocean voyages created the first global networks and transformed the Atlantic world, while much of Asia's economic power and many older trade patterns continued.
Continuity and change is an AP reasoning process. A strong answer names what changed, what stayed the same, and why.

records.title: Continuity and Change from 1450 to 1750
records.heading: What changed
records.text:
What changed
Global connection and the creation of Atlantic societies were the period's major changes.
For the first time, sea routes linked every inhabited continent. The Columbian Exchange transformed diets and environments, and American silver created a global economy centered on Chinese demand.
The Atlantic world changed most. European empires, epidemic disease, and the forced migration of millions of Africans produced new societies in the Americas.

What continued
European expansion added to, rather than replaced, many older patterns.
Asian merchants still carried most Indian Ocean trade. Chinese and Indian manufactured goods remained in demand worldwide, and land-based empires such as the Ottomans, Mughals, and Qing remained powerful.
Coerced labor also continued, though in new forms. Older systems of slavery and serfdom persisted while Atlantic chattel slavery expanded.
Because Asian states were strong and Asian goods were valuable, Europeans had to join existing trade networks rather than replace them.
Do not claim Europeans dominated the world by 1750. Their power was greatest in the Americas and at sea, not in Asia's interior.

records.title: The Enlightenment
records.text:
The Enlightenment
How Enlightenment thinkers applied reason to government and society, and how their ideas inspired reform movements.
Enlightenment thinkers used reason to question inherited authority, and their ideas about natural rights and consent fueled revolutions and reform movements.
The Scientific Revolution showed that reason and observation could explain nature. Thinkers of the 1700s applied the same methods to politics, religion, and society.
records.excerpt: How Enlightenment thinkers applied reason to government and society, and how their ideas inspired reform movements.

records.title: The Enlightenment
records.heading: Natural rights and the social contract
records.text:
Natural rights and the social contract
Natural rights and consent became the language of revolution.
John Locke argued in 1690 that people have natural rights to life, liberty, and property, and that government rests on the consent of the governed. If rulers violate those rights, the people may replace them.
Jean-Jacques Rousseau described a social contract in which citizens together form the general will. Montesquieu argued for the separation of powers among branches of government, and Voltaire championed religious tolerance and free expression.
Ideas that authority comes from the people undermined divine right, which encouraged colonists and subjects to justify revolt against kings.
Enlightenment thinkers did not all agree, and many did not apply their ideas to women, enslaved people, or colonized peoples.

records.title: Nationalism and Revolutions in the Period from 1750 to 1900
records.text:
Nationalism and Revolutions in the Period from 1750 to 1900
How the American, French, Haitian, and Latin American revolutions and the rise of nationalism reshaped states.
Enlightenment ideas and resentment of imperial or royal rule produced revolutions across the Atlantic world, while nationalism created new states in Europe.
By 1750, colonists and subjects had grievances about taxes, privilege, and exclusion. Enlightenment ideas gave those grievances a common language.

records.title: Nationalism and Revolutions in the Period from 1750 to 1900
records.heading: American and French revolutions
records.text:
American and French revolutions
Revolutions in North America and France applied Enlightenment ideas to real governments.
British colonists in North America declared independence in 1776, justifying revolt with natural rights and consent. Thomas Paine's pamphlet Common Sense helped persuade colonists to break with Britain.
In France, financial crisis and resentment of noble privilege led to revolution in 1789. The National Assembly issued the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen. Olympe de Gouges answered with a declaration of the rights of women in 1791.
Debt and taxes created conflict with rulers, and Enlightenment ideas turned that conflict into demands for new governments based on rights.

records.text:
Haiti and Latin America
Revolutions in the Americas ended colonial rule but left many inequalities intact.
In the French colony of Saint-Domingue, enslaved people revolted in 1791. Led by Toussaint Louverture and others, they won independence as Haiti in 1804, the only state founded by a successful revolt of enslaved people.
After Napoleon invaded Spain in 1808, creole leaders such as Simón Bolívar led independence wars that freed most of Spanish South America by 1825. Mexico became independent in 1821 and Brazil in 1822.
Latin American independence was led mostly by creole elites. It did not overturn the colonial social hierarchy.

Nationalism and unification
Nationalism created Italy and Germany and threatened multiethnic empires.
Nationalism is the belief that people who share a language, culture, and history should form one nation with its own state. It united some peoples and divided empires.
Italy was unified in 1861 through Cavour's diplomacy and Garibaldi's campaigns. Prussia's Otto von Bismarck unified Germany through war, proclaiming the German Empire in 1871.
Nationalism was not always democratic. Bismarck's unification was led by a conservative monarchy through war.

records.title: Industrial Revolution Begins
records.text:
Industrial Revolution Begins
Why industrial production began in Britain, and how machines, steam power, and factories transformed textile manufacturing.
Industrialization began in Britain because of coal and iron, agricultural change, capital, and overseas trade, and it transformed production through machines and factories.
Before 1750, goods were made by hand in homes and workshops, often in the putting-out system. Most energy came from muscles, water, wind, and wood.

records.title: Industrial Revolution Begins
records.heading: Why Britain
records.text:
Why Britain
A combination of resources, labor, capital, and global trade made Britain the first industrial nation.
Britain had coal and iron ore near rivers and ports. Agricultural improvements and the enclosure of common lands raised food output and pushed rural laborers toward towns, creating a workforce for factories.
Merchants had capital from trade, including the Atlantic trade, and banks and a stable government protected investments. Colonies supplied raw cotton and markets for finished goods.
Cheap coal, available labor, capital, and colonial markets made machines profitable, so British entrepreneurs invested in mechanized production first.
No single factor explains why industrialization began in Britain. Strong answers combine resources, labor, capital, and markets.

The spinning jenny and Richard Arkwright's water frame mechanized cotton spinning in the 1760s. Arkwright's mills brought workers under one roof on fixed hours, creating the factory system.

records.text:
Industrialization Spreads in the Period from 1750 to 1900
How industrialization spread to western Europe, the United States, Russia, and Japan, and how it hurt older manufacturing in places such as India.
Industrialization spread unevenly, making some countries powerful producers while older manufacturing centers such as India's textile industry declined.
Britain tried to keep its machines and methods secret, but skilled workers and plans spread, and other governments and entrepreneurs copied British success.

Industrialization spread from Britain, often with government support in late industrializers.
Belgium, France, and the German states began industrializing in the early 1800s. By 1900 Germany and the United States produced more steel than Britain.
Russia and Japan industrialized rapidly in the late 1800s with heavy government involvement. Japan became Asia's leading industrial power.

records.heading: Decline of older industries
records.text:
Decline of older industries
Industrial growth in some places caused decline in others.
Machine-made British cloth flooded markets in India, where hand spinners and weavers had supplied much of the world's cotton cloth. India became an exporter of raw cotton instead.
Shifts like this, sometimes called deindustrialization, turned some regions into suppliers of raw materials for industrial countries.
Cheap factory goods undersold handmade cloth, which ruined many artisans and pushed colonies to export raw materials instead.
Industrialization did not make every region richer. It often turned colonies into suppliers of raw materials.

New energy sources and machines transformed how goods were made and moved and how information traveled.
The steam engine was the key early technology. Later, steel, electricity, and chemistry produced a second wave of industrial change.

records.heading: Steam and transport
records.text:
Steam and transport
Steam and electricity shrank distances for goods and information.
James Watt's improvements to the steam engine made it far more efficient. Steam powered factories, then locomotives and ships. The Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened in 1830.
Railroads and steamships lowered transport costs and tied distant regions into national and global markets. The telegraph sent messages almost instantly; a transatlantic cable worked from 1866.
Cheaper and faster transport and communication expanded markets, which encouraged larger factories and more specialized production.

records.title: Industrialization: Government's Role from 1750 to 1900
records.text:
Industrialization: Government's Role from 1750 to 1900
How states such as Meiji Japan, Egypt under Muhammad Ali, and Russia promoted industrialization.
Some governments led industrialization themselves to strengthen their states against Western powers, with mixed results.
Late industrializers saw how industrial power let Britain and France dominate others. Governments that wanted to stay independent tried to build industry quickly.
records.excerpt: How states such as Meiji Japan, Egypt under Muhammad Ali, and Russia promoted industrialization.

records.title: Industrialization: Government's Role from 1750 to 1900
records.heading: Meiji Japan
records.text:
Meiji Japan
Meiji Japan shows how a government could drive rapid industrialization.
After the Meiji Restoration of 1868, Japan's leaders abolished the samurai class, created a conscript army, and sent students abroad to study Western science and government. The state built railroads, telegraph lines, and model factories.
The government later sold many factories to private owners, and some became zaibatsu, large family-controlled business groups.
Fear of Western domination led Meiji leaders to build industry and a modern army, which made Japan a major power by 1900.
records.excerpt: Meiji Japan shows how a government could drive rapid industrialization.

records.title: Industrialization: Government's Role from 1750 to 1900
records.heading: Egypt and Russia
records.text:
Egypt and Russia
State-led industrialization had mixed results depending on resources and foreign pressure.
Muhammad Ali, governor of Egypt from 1805 to 1848, built state factories and required farmers to grow cotton for export. After European powers forced him to reduce his army in 1841, many factories closed.
In Russia, the state built railroads, including the Trans-Siberian Railway begun in 1891, and encouraged heavy industry through foreign investment and tariffs.
State support did not guarantee success. Egypt's factories struggled against British competition and European pressure.

records.title: Economic Developments and Innovations in the Industrial Age
records.text:
Economic Developments and Innovations in the Industrial Age
How laissez-faire ideas, limited liability, stock markets, and transnational businesses changed economies.
New economic ideas and institutions, from Adam Smith's free-market arguments to limited liability and global banks, supported industrial capitalism.
Mercantilism dominated European economic thinking before 1750. Industrialization encouraged new arguments for free markets and new ways to raise capital.
records.excerpt: How laissez-faire ideas, limited liability, stock markets, and transnational businesses changed economies.

records.title: Economic Developments and Innovations in the Industrial Age
records.heading: Laissez-faire ideas
records.text:
Laissez-faire ideas
Free-market ideas challenged mercantilism and shaped industrial economies.
Adam Smith argued in 1776 that the division of labor and free markets would increase wealth. Laissez-faire capitalism held that government should interfere little in the economy.
Critics pointed to monopolies, harsh working conditions, and economic crises, and some called for regulation.
Laissez-faire was an argument, not a description of reality. Governments still passed tariffs, built railroads, and regulated some industries.

records.heading: New financial institutions

New financial institutions
New financial tools mobilized capital for large industrial firms.
Limited liability, introduced in Britain in 1855, meant investors could lose only what they had invested. Stock exchanges grew as more people bought shares.
Banks and businesses operated across borders. The Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation, founded in 1865, financed trade across Asia.
Limited liability lowered investors' risk, which drew more capital into companies and allowed larger enterprises.

records.title: Reactions to the Industrial Economy from 1750 to 1900
records.text:
Reactions to the Industrial Economy from 1750 to 1900
How workers, socialists, and governments responded to industrial capitalism, and how China and the Ottoman Empire attempted reform.
Industrial capitalism produced workers' movements, socialist ideas, and government reforms, while states facing industrial powers attempted reforms of their own.
Long hours, low wages, and dangerous conditions led workers to organize. Thinkers debated whether reform or revolution was the answer.

records.title: Reactions to the Industrial Economy from 1750 to 1900
records.heading: Workers and reform
records.text:
Workers and reform
Workers organized, and governments gradually responded with reforms.
Luddites smashed machines in Britain between 1811 and 1816. Over time, workers formed labor unions to bargain for better wages and hours. Chartists demanded voting rights for all men.
Britain's Factory Act of 1833 limited child labor, and voting rights expanded in 1867 and 1884.

records.heading: Socialism and Marxism
records.text:
Socialism and Marxism
Marxism offered a revolutionary critique of industrial capitalism.
Socialists argued that workers or society as a whole should own the means of production. Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels published the Communist Manifesto in 1848, arguing that history was a struggle between classes and predicting a workers' revolution.
Harsh factory conditions and inequality led critics to argue that capitalism itself must change, which produced socialist and communist movements.
Not all socialists were revolutionaries. Many sought change through elections, unions, and laws.

Reforms in China and the Ottoman Empire borrowed Western methods but faced resistance and limited success.
China's Self-Strengthening Movement of the 1860s built arsenals and shipyards while keeping Confucian institutions. Defeat by Japan in 1895 exposed its limits.
The Ottoman Tanzimat reforms of 1839 to 1876 reorganized the army, courts, and schools and declared legal equality for all subjects.

records.title: Society and the Industrial Age
records.text:
Society and the Industrial Age
How industrialization created new social classes, changed family and gender roles, and transformed cities.
Industrialization created a new working class and middle class, changed family and gender roles, and produced crowded cities with new problems.
Factory work separated home from workplace. Millions moved from countryside to city in search of work.
records.excerpt: How industrialization created new social classes, changed family and gender roles, and transformed cities.

records.title: Society and the Industrial Age
records.heading: New social classes
records.text:
New social classes
Industrialization reshaped social hierarchy around wages and property rather than birth.
The industrial working class labored in factories and mines for wages, often twelve hours a day or more. A growing middle class of managers, professionals, and shopkeepers gained wealth and influence.
Middle-class writers praised hard work, thrift, and self-improvement. Samuel Smiles's Self-Help, published in 1859, became a best seller.

records.heading: Family life and cities
records.text:
Family life and cities
Urban industrial life brought new opportunities and serious hardships.
Women and children worked in mills for lower pay than men. Middle-class families often followed the ideal of separate spheres, in which men earned wages and women managed the home.
Rapid urbanization meant that cities grew faster than housing and sanitation. Crowded tenements and polluted water spread diseases such as cholera, which led to public health reforms later in the century.
Rapid migration to cities overwhelmed housing and water systems, which spread disease and eventually pushed governments to build sewers and clean water supplies.
Separate spheres was a middle-class ideal. Most working-class women still had to work for wages.

records.title: Continuity and Change in the Industrial Age
records.text:
Continuity and Change in the Industrial Age
What changed and what continued as revolutions and industrialization transformed the world from 1750 to 1900.
Revolutions and industrialization brought rapid change, yet agriculture, monarchy, and many inequalities continued.
Continuity and change is an AP reasoning process. Strong answers weigh both.

records.title: Continuity and Change in the Industrial Age
records.heading: Weighing change and continuity
records.text:
Weighing change and continuity
The period combined dramatic change with deep continuities.
Ideas of natural rights and nationalism spread, new nations formed, and machines and fossil fuels transformed production. Global trade grew and connected regions more tightly.
Yet most people still farmed, many states remained monarchies, and industrial wealth was concentrated in a few countries. Women, colonized peoples, and many workers remained excluded from political rights.
Do not overstate change. A strong answer names what stayed the same as well as what changed.
